title: Structures, Unions and Padding
quickIdea: A struct places its members one after another in declaration order, inserting padding so each lands on a suitable boundary; a union places them all at offset zero, so only the last one written is readable.
remember: sizeof(struct) is at least the sum of the member sizes and usually more. Each member is aligned to its own requirement, commonly its own size; the struct's alignment is its largest member's, and the total is rounded up to a multiple of it.
Reordering members can change the size: char, int, char needs padding after the first char, while char, char, int needs none.
sizeof(union) is the size of its largest member, rounded up to the union's alignment. All members start at the same address, so writing one overwrites the bytes of the others.
Member access is . on a struct and -> on a pointer to one; (*q).x and q->x are the same object.
A struct is assignable and is copied when passed by value, padding included. An array inside a struct is copied element by element; a pointer inside one is copied as an address, not followed.
Casting a struct pointer to char * changes the arithmetic, not the object: (char *)q + 1 moves one byte inside the struct, while q + 1 would move a whole struct.

example.prompt: struct Ournode { char x, y, z; }; struct Ournode p = {'1', '0', 'a' + 2}; struct Ournode *q = &p; printf("%c, %c", *((char *)q + 1), *((char *)q + 2));
example.work: 'a' + 2 is the character 'c'. The three chars sit in consecutive bytes at offsets 0, 1 and 2. (char *)q makes the pointer step one byte at a time, so (char *)q + 1 addresses the second byte and (char *)q + 2 the third. Dereferencing them gives '0' and 'c', and %c prints characters without quotes.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2018 Q.2 is this program and the answer is 0, c. GATE CSE 2000's struct-inside-a-union question is the size version of the same layout idea. The distractors in both are the ones you get by forgetting the cast, which would step a whole struct, or by counting a union as the sum of its members.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: What is sizeof for struct { char c; int i; char d; } with 4-byte ints and the usual alignment?
variations.answer: 12: c at 0, three padding bytes, i at 4, d at 8, and three bytes of tail padding to round the total up to the struct's alignment of 4.
variations.why: The padding half of the same layout question; the 2018 question tests offsets and the 2000 one tests sizes.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why can a union not hold two members' values at the same time?
variations.answer: Because all its members share one storage region starting at the same address, so writing one member overwrites the bytes the previous member occupied.
variations.why: The property that makes a union's size the maximum and not the sum.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: union U { float y; long z; } with float 4 and long 8 bytes - what is sizeof(union U), and what is sizeof(struct { float y; long z; }) ignoring alignment?
variations.answer: 8 for the union and 12 for the struct.
variations.why: The one-word difference that changes the answer, which is the whole point of the 2000 question.

trap.what: Assuming that casting a struct pointer to char * lets you walk to the next struct.
trap.why: The cast changes the pointer's type, and with it the step size. (char *)q + 1 addresses the second byte of the same object, while q + 1 addresses the next struct, sizeof(struct) bytes away, which usually does not exist.
trap.counterexample: In GATE CSE 2018 Q.2, *(q + 1) would read outside p entirely, while *((char *)q + 1) reads p's second byte, which is '0'.

check.question: struct S { char a; char b; int c; }; with 4-byte ints and no reordering, what is sizeof(struct S)?
check.explanation: a at 0, b at 1, two padding bytes so that c starts on a multiple of 4, then c at 4 to 7. The total 8 is already a multiple of the struct's alignment, 4.

visual.title: Structures, Unions and Enumerations: layout, padding and type punning
covers: offset = ceil(running / align) * align, then running = offset + size
sizeof = ceil(end / largest align) * largest align
a union's size is its largest member rounded up to its largest alignment
padding bytes have unspecified values, so memcmp on a struct compares them
